leads.title: Social physiology: the hidden health cost of eating alone, according to science
leads.summary: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM A study published in Science Advances found that eating the same meal with a family member or friend produces measurably better blood sugar control than eating it alone. In experiments with 108 participants, researchers at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem measured glycemic response after eating roughly 100 grams of white-wheat bread under two conditions: alone, and alongside a family member or friend. When participants ate with someone they knew, blood sugar spiked less and returned to baseline faster. The difference was measurable, and it had nothing to do with what was on the plate. “Blood sugar regulation is not just about what we eat, but who we eat with,” says lead researcher Shir Atzil. “Our relationships have an active biological role in our physical well-being.” The body as an open system The researchers call the framework behind this “social physiology,” and it’s a genuine departure from how most of us think about health. The standard model treats the body as a closed system that regulates itself. Social physiology says human bodies are designed to operate in coordination with other bodies, that the people around us, especially close ones, are part of the regulatory environment. “We used to think of the body as an isolated system that regulates itself,” Atzil says . “Our findings show that human physiology is inherently social. Being close to someone you love lowers the physical energy your body spends on regulating itself. This gives us a direct metabolic benefit to being together and reveals a core evolutionary reason why humans form bonds in the first place: our bodies run better together.” The glucose finding wasn’t the only one. leads.title: Inside Mumbai's Dirtiest Beach? 18000 KG Of Waste (Shocking😳)
leads.summary: Mumbai’s ocean is drowning in plastic. And we’re running out of places to hide it. Every year, around 5 million kg of plastic drains out of Mumbai into the Arabian Sea. Most of it stays there. This time, it didn't. We put 1,500+ volunteers on one shoreline for a single day and pulled 18,000 kg of marine plastic off the sand. But the real story started after the bags were full. We followed that waste into a recycling facility, watched it get washed, sorted and remade, and then saw it walk back into classrooms as benches for children who needed them. That's the whole chain. Trash, to truck, to bench, to kid. Nobody cut a single step out of it. This is The Better India's Civic Sense Revolution and it doesn't end at the beach. 👇🏻 Tell us in the comments: Which Mumbai beach should we clean next? leads.title: This Truck Eats Garbage Before It Reaches Landfills
leads.summary: #After witnessing a cow die with nearly 5 kg of plastic in its stomach, Akshay Deshpande set out to understand India’s waste crisis. Following more than 780 interviews, he founded Switcheko Sustainability in Hyderabad to explore a better way to manage waste. The initiative developed a 22-foot solar-powered mobile waste-processing truck that sorts, shreds and processes waste on-site before it reaches a landfill. The project reports having processed over 1 lakh kg of waste, reached more than 4 lakh people and created opportunities for around 180 women. It brings waste management closer to communities while highlighting the importance of reducing plastic pollution and improving waste segregation. From one heartbreaking discovery to an innovative approach to sustainable waste management, this story shows how local ideas can address bigger environmental challenges. Could mobile waste-processing trucks help Indian cities manage garbage more efficiently?
